questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.problem:
Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for
  $f(x)=5{x}^{3}+3x$ on the interval $[0,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0,2]$ and differentiable on $(0,2),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (0,2)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-(0)} \\  & =\frac{(5\cdot {2}^{3}+3\cdot 2)-(5\cdot {0}^{3}+3\cdot 0)}{2} \\  & =\frac{46-0}{2} \\  & =23.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{3}+3x)=15{x}^{2}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=15{c}^{2}+3.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}15{c}^{2}+3 & =23 \\ 15{c}^{2} & =20 \\ {c}^{2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ c & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c\in (0,2)$, we discard the negative value, therefore $c=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Functions That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,8]?$

- $g(x)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}}$
- $s(x)=(x-2)^{2}$
- $h(x)=\frac{1}{x-3}$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,8],$ the function must be continuous on $[1,8]$ and differentiable on $(1,8).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $g(x)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}}$ is continuous on $[1,8]$ and has a cusp only at $x=0,$ which is outside $[1,8],$ hence it is differentiable on $(1,8).$ Therefore, $g(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $s(x)=(x-2)^{2}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it  is continuous on $[1,8]$ and differentiable on $(1,8).$ Therefore, $s(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function  $h(x)=\frac{1}{x-3}$ is not defined at $x=3$, so it is not continuous at $x=3$, which means it is not continuous on $[1,8].$ Therefore, $h(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only functions I and II satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,8].$

questions.problem: Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,0]?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,0],$ the function must be continuous on $[-4,0]$ and differentiable on $(-4,0).$

First, notice that the function $v(x)$ is continuous on $[-4,0]$ and differentiable on $(-4,0),$ so it satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Let's check each of the other functions individually.

- The function $r(x)$ is continuous on $[-4,0]$ but has a corner point at $x=-1.$ Hence, $r(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=-1,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(-4,0).$ Therefore, $r(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $s(x)$ has a jump discontinuity at $x=-2.$ Hence, $s(x)$ is not continuous on $[-4,0].$ Therefore, $s(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $t(x)$ is continuous on $[-4,0]$ but has a corner point at $x=-2.$ Hence, $t(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=-2,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(-4,0).$ Therefore, $t(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $u(x)$  has a vertical asymptote at $x=-1.$ Hence, $u(x)$ is not continuous on $[-4,0].$ Therefore, $u(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0,6]$ and differentiable on $(0,6),$  hence we can apply the mean value theorem.  

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (0,6)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=6$ into the above gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(6)-f(0)}{6-0} \\  & =\frac{({6}^{2}-4\cdot 6+2)-({0}^{2}-4\cdot 0+2)}{6} \\  & =\frac{14-2}{6} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-4x+2)=2x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=2c-4.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2c-4 & =2 \\ c & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
